To support the allegation of violation of these provisions of the Charter, the Complainants invoke the numerous refusals to authorise meetings and the actual prevention by the police. They conclude that these acts violate their freedoms of association and assembly.

The Complainants allege that the refusal of authorisation to function, the refusal to execute court decisions and the various obstacles to holding their activities violate the right to participate freely in the government of their country.

In response to the Complainants' allegations on this point, the Respondent State argues that the assessment of equality can be made only in the presence of two identical situations. The State considers in this regard that there can be no question of discrimination when one considers the flourishing of political parties, of which at least 288 are authorised to operate freely in Cameroon.

Concerning the specific case of the UPC, the Respondent State reports that after the adoption of Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990 this party applied for and obtained authorisation in the same way as many other political parties. The State nevertheless indicates that the Complainants never submitted an application for authorisation and that there is no political party called UPC-MANIDEM or UPC-KODOCK.

The Respondent State mentions, however, that in the wake of the above-cited Law liberalising political activity in Cameroon, dissensions within the UPC gave rise to several factions; that it is in the midst of these dissensions that the administration received in January 1991 an application for authorisation of the legal existence of the UPC party, to which a favourable response was given on 12 February 1991.

The State argues that such an authorisation then constituted an automatic bar to any other application concerning the same acronym and that, consequently, the application of UPC-MANIDEM had been rejected whereas an authorisation had been issued to the party called MANIDEM. Such a practice, according to the Respondent State, is well recognised by the Commission, which considers that a right may be limited for the needs of the organisation of the State.

As regards the Complainants' judicial disputes, the State rejects any implication, indicating that the administration never brought a lawsuit against the Complainants nor participated in any proceedings involving them. As for the prohibitions of meetings and the related police interventions, the State argues that they are well founded in that it cannot be possible to authorise the activities of a party that operates without legal authorisation.

The Respondent State concludes that the allegation of violation of the right to a fair trial is unfounded by referring to the decision rendered by the Littoral Court of Appeal in favour of the Complainants but also to that of the Administrative Chamber annulling that of the administration for abuse of power.

In response to the argument based on the absence of independence of the judiciary, the State argues that the fact that the President of the Republic is "guarantor of the Magistracy" in no way infringes such independence given that the judges of the bench are subject only to the law and their conscience.

According to the Respondent State, the Complainants being unable to prove the legal existence of an authorised political party, they cannot claim the enjoyment of any of the rights whose violation they allege.

Relative to political participation, the Respondent State argues that there was no violation of this right given that the Complainants did not meet the legal criterion for investiture by a political party authorised to participate in an election in Cameroon. The State further indicates that the UPC did participate in all electoral consultations in Cameroon since 1992.

Under Article 2 of the African Charter, every individual is entitled to the enjoyment of the rights guaranteed in the Charter without distinction of any kind, notably ... political or any other opinion ... or other status. As for Article 3, it stipulates that "1. Every individual shall be equal before the law. 2. Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law". From the wording of these two provisions, it emerges that whereas Article 3 guarantees the right to equality, Article 2 defines the scope of this right by prescribing non-discrimination as the principal prohibition by which respect for the right to equality must be judged. In other words, Article 3 guarantees a right and Article 2 lays down a prohibition. When the two provisions are invoked concomitantly, as is the case here, the allegation of their violation must be examined jointly.

Discrimination is an unlawful or unjustified differentiation, that is, one based on one of the distinctions cited in Article 2 of the Charter, in this case political opinion, here alleged, or other status. As regards equal protection of the law, in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Another v. Zimbabwe, the Commission interprets it as the right recognised for every person to have equal access to the courts and to be treated equally by them both in procedures and in substance. It goes without saying that the Charter recognises as inherent in the right to equal protection of the law a tacit guarantee of non-discrimination in proceedings before the courts and in the application of the law to persons in an identical or similar situation.

This being so, as soon as the discrimination proscribed in Article 2 is constituted, there is necessarily a breach of the right to equality protected in Article 3. In the present Communication, the Commission will therefore examine the allegations of discrimination made by the Complainants in order to conclude whether or not there is a violation of Articles 2 and 3 depending on whether the discrimination is constituted or not.

The Commission agrees with the Respondent State that differentiation necessarily implies a comparator. However, this comparator could be explicit or implicit, known or presumed. In any event, as soon as the differentiation is based on political opinion or any other distinction, it is presumed unlawful until proven otherwise.

In the present case, it emerges from the arguments invoked by the Parties that Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990 on the liberalisation of political life in Cameroon placed the Complainants in a position of equality with all the other citizens and leaders of political parties existing at the time. The grievances raised by the Complainants rather relate to the enjoyment of this equality in practice, the violation of which they argue by alleging a series of discriminations.

In this regard, the Commission notes that after the entry into force of the above-mentioned law, the two political parties in existence in Cameroon were that of the Complainants, the UPC, and the Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM). The Complainants then addressed to the administration in December 1990 a correspondence indicating the intention of the already existing UPC party to resume its activities in application of the provisions of the new law. However, they were met with a rejection for lack of legal existence. On the other hand, the administration had subsequently authorised to function a new political party also called UPC (however under the leadership of KODOCK and others) whose leaders submitted an application for authorisation only on 4 January 1991.

The Commission finds that in such a situation, the Complainants' UPC had at least two comparators, notably the CPDM and the UPC subsequently authorised by the administration, which will be identified here as UPC-KODOCK for ease of reference. With the CPDM, the Complainants' UPC, pre-existing the Law of 19 December 1990, had an identity of enjoyment of the implicit authorisation granted by the new law in the sense that there was no need for the Complainants to submit an application for authorisation, still less to obtain one, to carry out their activities.

In its brief on the merits, the Respondent State indeed cites the provisions of Article 21 of the said Law under which "political parties that exist legally at the date of promulgation of this law do not have to apply for a new authorisation". The State does not contest the existence of the Complainants' UPC at the reference date, namely that of the entry into force of the new law. The manifest conclusion is that the new law entailed authorisation to resume functioning and thus automatic legal existence of the Complainants' UPC from 19 December 1990. In these circumstances, two major legal situations had formed: that which prevailed at the liberalisation of the functioning of political parties in 1990 and that which prevailed thereafter.

In the first situation, the Commission notes that in its brief on the merits, the Respondent State indicates that several parties existing before and after independence applied for and obtained an authorisation, without however citing the parties pre-existing the adoption of the new law. Be that as it may, the Commission considers that the relevant provisions of the said law equate the tacit recognition of the parties pre-existing the entry into force of the law with the recognition by required authorisation of the parties created thereafter, notably the Cameroonian Socialist Union, the Cameroonian Democratic Party and even the UPC registered under the leadership of KODOCK and others cited by the State in its brief on the merits. It must therefore be noted that these political parties were valid comparators and that, by requiring the Complainants' UPC to obtain an authorisation already granted by the new law but by authorising the said comparators in an identical situation, the Respondent State applied a different treatment. For discrimination to be constituted, it would in addition have to be unjustified.

On the justification of the difference in treatment, the Respondent State alleges the vigour of Cameroonian democracy proved by the existence of 288 political parties authorised to function. In addition, the State argues that, having already issued an authorisation to function to the UPC (KODOCK) on 12 February 1991, there was a legal impediment to the issuance of a subsequent authorisation to the UPC (MANIDEM).

Concerning the number of political parties authorised to function in Cameroon, the Commission notes that it cannot in any way justify the difference in treatment to which the Complainants' party was subjected. As for the legal impediment put forward by the Respondent State, the Commission considers that the date of authorisation of 12 February 1991 indicated by the State is well after that of 19 December 1990 on which the Complainants' UPC obtained full legality to function without the need for any express authorisation from the administration. The State does not contest this established fact and does not provide proof to the contrary that its administration rejected the Complainants' letter of information on grounds of lack of legal existence. On the finding of the absence of justification for the difference in treatment, the Commission concludes that discrimination is constituted concerning the legal situation prevailing before the entry into force of Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990.

The second situation is that which prevailed after the adoption of the new law and which required an express authorisation to operate as a political party in Cameroon. The Commission notes that the Respondent State, having already granted an authorisation to the KODOCK wing of the UPC, decided, by letter of 22 September 1992, to reject the Complainants' application to carry out political activities under the aegis of a party called UPC-MANIDEM for double use of the acronym UPC. Seized by the Complainants, the Supreme Court had then, by order dated 16 December 1992, annulled the said letter, thus enshrining the legal existence of the party UPC-MANIDEM.

However, the authorities of the Respondent State have, by various means, hindered the functioning of the party UPC-MANIDEM authorised by the Supreme Court. It emerges from the information contained in the file that despite the decision of the Supreme Court of 16 December 1992, the security forces of the Respondent State intervened through arrests, sequestrations and other forms of harassment to prevent meetings of UPC-MANIDEM organised in August 1995, August 2008, August 2011, February 2013 and August 2014.

The State does not contest the veracity of the refusals to authorise meetings and the police interventions. To justify the various impediments thus mentioned, the Respondent State alleges the lack of legal existence of the UPC (MANIDEM) for double use of the acronym UPC. In this regard, the Commission notes that the decision of the Supreme Court dating from 1992 and recalled above establishes the legality of the UPC (MANIDEM). While it is true that an action was brought in court against the double use of the acronym UPC, the appeal on points of law lodged in this regard by the Complainants before the Supreme Court against the decisions of the courts of first instance and appeal has remained without action since 1998. The decisions of the Supreme Court being final, they have the force of res judicata until the same court rules on a new application concerning the same case. It goes without saying that the order of the highest court authorising the functioning of the UPC (MANIDEM) remains valid. This validity defeats the Respondent State's argument based on the lack of legal existence of the UPC (MANIDEM).

In these circumstances, it remains to be determined to what extent the acts of the administration reported above were discriminatory and how equality was broken. On this point, the Commission refers to the Respondent State's brief on the merits, in which it clearly indicates that subsequent to the adoption of Law No. 1990/056, several political parties such as the Cameroonian Social Union (USC), the Cameroon People's Party (CPP) and the Cameroonian Democratic Party (PDC) obtained an authorisation and freely conduct their activities. It follows that the impediments to which the UPC (MANIDEM) was subjected are unjustified and constitute discrimination. There was therefore a breach of the right to equal protection of the law, in this case because the security forces of the Respondent State should have guaranteed the Complainants the same right to hold their meetings and other activities as is the case for all the other political parties cited by the Respondent State. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter have been violated.

Under the provisions of Article 7(1)(d), every individual has the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court. In its jurisprudence on the reasonable time of administration of justice, the Commission carries out an assessment on a case-by-case basis, notably on the basis of factors such as the facts of the case, the situation of the Complainant and the domestic law of the Respondent State. In any event, it is in light of the circumstances of the case and the complexity of the issues brought before the courts that the reasonable or unreasonable nature of the time of administration of justice should be determined.

In the present case, the Parties agree that, in the case of UPC (KODOCK) against the Complainants tried at first instance by the High Court of Wouri, the appellate judge rendered a decision but that the appeal on points of law lodged before the Supreme Court of Cameroon in 1998 had not been followed up as of the date of the present examination. The Commission notes that the main issue in dispute before the domestic courts is that of the Complainants' right to participate in the political life of their country. On a question of such great importance, and considering that the appeal before the Supreme Court concerned the mere refusal of the Court of Appeal to rule on a counterclaim, the Commission considers that a period of 18 years is not reasonable.

On the argument based on the lack of impartiality of the domestic courts, the Commission is of the view, with the European Court of Human Rights when it considers in Cubber v. Belgium that the impartiality of judges is the fundamental condition of the "confidence which the courts must inspire in the courts in a democratic society". The Commission notes that as such impartiality stems mainly from the impression that the judicial system gives to the litigant and therefore from a logic relating mainly to appearances. Given the subtle nature of its expression, it is therefore in light of the theory of appearances that the jurisprudence assesses impartiality.

In its relevant jurisprudence, the European Court distinguishes a twofold impartiality: subjective of the judge and objective of the court. In Remli v. France, for example, the Court considers, concerning the subjective approach, that the personal conviction of a given judge on a given occasion must be sought. In that case, the applicant of Maghrebi origin had lodged a request for legitimate suspicion after one of the assize jurors declared, outside the hearing, "what is more, I am racist". The Court had then held that the Assize Court's failure to take this legitimate suspicion into account in the composition of the assize jury left the legitimacy of the suspicion of the Court's partiality standing. To assess the subjective impartiality of the assize judges, the Court considers as a determining element "whether the applicant's apprehensions can be regarded as objectively justified" and that there is a duty for the court concerned to examine any challenge arising as to its impartiality insofar as such a challenge is serious.

As for the objective approach, it consists in establishing that other functions of a judge are likely to give rise to a prejudgment of partiality or the appearance of partiality. For example, in the above-cited Cubber case, the Court condemns the fact that a prosecution magistrate may sit in a trial court. In Mancel and Branquart, it concludes that the Court of Cassation, which had already ruled on a first appeal, was biased. On the basis of the "theory of appearances" adopted in Piersack v. Belgium, the Court places the burden of proof on the applicant given that the presumption of partiality is only rebuttable. In sum, the judge must be free of any prejudice. The necessity of such an absence of prejudice shows clearly from the position of the European Court when it says in M v. France that it suffices to note that "... the impartiality of the Court of Cassation could give rise to serious doubts and that the applicant's fears could be regarded as objectively justified".

In the present case, as regards subjective impartiality, the Complainant puts forward the fact that different courts reached the same conclusion - erroneous in his understanding - on the same question. In this regard, the Commission notes that on the same dispute concerning the validity of the protection of the acronym and emblems of the UPC (KODOCK), the High Court of Wouri, the Littoral Court of Appeal and the Court of First Instance of Douala-Bonanjo reached the same decision to reject his counterclaim for annulment of the acronym and emblems of the UPC (KODOKC), apparently for lack of capacity.

The Commission notes that such lack of capacity is only apparent since in reality, instead of a rejection for lack of capacity, it was a matter of a lack of reasoning and a denial of justice. As proof, the relevant grounds of the decision of the High Court of Wouri read "whereas the grounds put forward in support of this (counter)claim prove unfounded; whereas it is therefore appropriate to dismiss the defendant party from this claim". The Commission notes that this reasoning not revealing a lack of jurisdiction, the court did not rule on its jurisdiction, still less did it give reasons for the lack of foundation of the Complainants' claim. In addition, the State does not contest the Complainants' allegation that the High Court, which enjoys full jurisdiction, cannot use as a pretext a material incapacity to refuse to rule on the counterclaim concerning the nullity of the protection of the acronym UPC.

With regard to the Court of Appeal, the Commission notes that it considered that it could not "examine the other grounds without having examined the question of incapacity". Consequently, the Court concluded as to the jurisdiction of the first judge only on the amount of the claim, which had been raised, by oral submissions, from the three million CFA francs requested in the originating application to 350 million, that is beyond the legal limit of 5 million. The Court's decision to overturn the judgment appealed against therefore drew its ground only from this sole failure to respect the subject-matter jurisdiction of the lower court judge. In addition, the Commission notes that, having annulled the conviction by the High Court of one of the Complainants, Mr Michel NDOH, the Court of Appeal nevertheless refused to rule on the nullity of the protection of the acronym UPC, the use of which was nevertheless the main ground of the said conviction. The appellate judge had, in any event, dispensed with all the other grounds raised by the parties.

It can easily be concluded that the two courts simply omitted or refused to rule on the counterclaim lodged by the Complainants. In addition, the fact that a third court, in this case the Court of First Instance of Doula-Bonanjo, adopted the same position in the same dispute otherwise brought may form the basis of a legitimate suspicion of prejudgment, bias and therefore of absence of impartiality. The arguments put forward by the Complainants in this regard were duly recalled above.

The Commission considers that, given the complex nature of impartiality, which is difficult to prove, notably subjective impartiality, appearances constitute the most reliable recourse since one cannot materially probe the inner motivations of the judge, notably his intimate conviction. In particular, in constitutional democracies governed by the separation of powers, the independence of the judge should be assessed in light of the adage "justice must not only be done, it must also be seen to be done". The European Court of Human Rights agrees when it concludes in Konstas v. Greece for example, that public statements by members of the government, mainly the minister of justice, necessarily give the public the impression that there is interference with the course of justice. The guarantee of impartiality must consequently necessarily be assessed in light of the independence of the judicial system, notably vis-à-vis the executive and legislative powers.

Relative to this independence of the courts, the Commission concluded, in the Meldrum v. Zimbabwe case, that it necessarily presupposes the absence of pressure or interference. In the same logic, when examining the Wetsh'okonda Koso and Others v. Democratic Republic of Congo case, the Commission considered that the independence of the courts must in any event be assessed with regard to the executive power. As factors of assessment, the Commission retained, among others, appointment, security of tenure, protection against external pressures and the perception of independence. In addition, and very notably, the Commission concluded that there was an absence of independence of the judiciary in Gunme and Others v. Cameroon on the finding that the Higher Judicial Council was chaired by the President of the Republic assisted by the Minister of Justice.

Likewise, the European Court of Human Rights holds, notably in the leading decisions Medvedyev v. France and Moulin v. France, that the public prosecutor is disqualified from exercising judicial functions notably for lack of independence vis-à-vis the executive power.

In the present case, the Commission notes that whereas the Constitution of the Respondent State establishes the separation of powers as a central pillar of the rule of law, the provisions of Article 37(3) of the same Constitution invest the President of the Republic as the guarantor of the independence of the judiciary. In addition, the President of the Republic is also the President of the Higher Judicial Council, the body in charge of the appointment of magistrates, the management of their careers and the functioning of the judicial system.

Moreover, turning to other elements of legitimate suspicion that were not contested by the Respondent State, the Commission notes that the Complainants put forward that "the judges themselves, outside of court, declared themselves sorry to have rendered decisions against the law and their conscience, in order to comply with the injunctions of the government and openly complain of the absence of independence of the judicial system in Cameroon".

In such a system where one power intervenes so directly and decisively in the functioning of another power, the legitimate suspicion is well founded by the theory of appearances examined above. In the present case, it is established that the Complainants' UPC has always been a party historically opposed to the ruling party which largely controls the executive power. The Commission also noted that, in their multiple attempts to peacefully carry out their political activities as UPC or UPC-MANIDEM, the Complainants suffered numerous setbacks despite the decisions rendered in their favour by the domestic courts, including the Supreme Court.

In response to the allegation of partiality, the Respondent State argues that the fact that the administrative judge rendered a decision in favour of the Complainants well attests to the absence of interference by the executive power in the functioning of the courts. The Commission notes that this decision mentioned by the Respondent State cannot by itself suffice to demonstrate the impartiality of the courts. As the facts attest, the judge concerned was a few months from his retirement, which is likely to justify the freedom of mind that characterised the impartiality of his positions. Moreover, as examined above, impartiality can be both subjective, targeting a single judge, or objective, targeting the whole court ruling on the case, several courts or even the whole judicial system as the case may be. By the benefit of all these grounds, the Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter have been violated.

The provisions whose violation is alleged guarantee the rights to the dissemination of one's opinions, to assembly, to association and to political participation. The State argues that the lack of legal authorisation to function of their political party renders the Complainants unfit for the enjoyment of the rights thus guaranteed.

The Commission considers that, in view of the Complainants' claims, the rights whose violation is alleged are inherent in the functioning of a political party. It is therefore appropriate to rule on them jointly, by examining first the allegation of violation of the right to political participation.

The right to political participation is protected by the provisions of Article 13(1) of the Charter, which guarantee the rights to elect and to be elected in accordance with the law. As the Respondent State indicates in its brief on the merits, the benefit of these rights is effective in Cameroon only within the framework of authorised political parties so that an authorisation entails enjoyment of the rights concerned.

In examining the essential components of the right to political participation, the Commission decided in Mamboundou v. Gabon that it includes, among other things, transparency in the participation of candidates and political parties in animating political life and in elections. In addition, in the case of Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria the Commission considered that the right to political participation: "... implies, among other things, the right to vote for the representative of one's choice (...) and that the annulment of the results constitutes a violation of this right". Finally, in its decision Lawyers for Human Rights v. Swaziland it concluded that "the adoption of a law prohibiting the creation of political parties seriously undermines the capacity of citizens to participate in the conduct of the affairs of their country, in violation of Article 13 of the Charter".

In light of these precedents, the Commission notes that the assessment of the free nature of political participation should be made in light of factors linked to the conduct of the Respondent State in the face of citizens' initiatives aimed at the enjoyment of this right. In this case, since such enjoyment is subject to compliance with the law, it will be a matter of determining whether citizens enjoyed free access once they had complied with it.

In the present case, the Commission finds that the Complainants' UPC, pre-existing the new law, was prevented from functioning. In addition, the UPC-MANIDEM subsequently authorised by the Supreme Court was the subject of constant harassment violating the authority of the order of the highest court. The unreasonable length of the proceedings aimed at restoring such authority completed the crystallisation of the violation. The arguments developed on the violation of the right to equality are applicable with regard to the right to political participation. By the benefit of these arguments, the Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 13(1) have been violated.

On the right to the dissemination of one's opinions, the Commission notes that it constitutes the very essence of the creation of a political party whose aim is to win power by disseminating its political ideas, opinions and programme among the electorate. As for the freedoms of assembly and association, they constitute the guarantee that makes the dissemination of political opinions possible. When political parties cannot meet freely or citizens cannot freely form political parties, the right to disseminate their political opinions is mortgaged. These violations being subsequent to that of the right to political participation, it must be concluded that Articles 9, 10 and 11 of the Charter have been violated.

The Commission having received the Complainants' arguments, it is appropriate to examine the related claims. Where, as is the case here, the Complainant does not produce the specific scales for determining the damages requested, the Commission has discretion to quantify the reparation or refer to the domestic bodies of the Respondent State. In any event, reparation must be just, adequate, effective, sufficient, appropriate, victim-oriented and proportionate to the prejudice suffered.

On the full reinstatement of the UPC created in 1948, the Commission notes that it could be technically complex to grant it given that the name UPC has already been attributed to another political group which has made full use of it over time. The main object of the Complaint being the enjoyment of the right to political participation, the Commission considers that the authorisation to exercise this right under the name UPC MANIDEM is capable of providing for it. It goes without saying that the Complainants must be able to enjoy their full civil and political rights, in this case that of political participation under the banner of the political formation they created and which is legal under the law in force.

As for compensation for prejudice, the facts of the case sufficiently prove that significant prejudice was caused to the Complainants. It is appropriate to require reparation for it. The Commission, For these reasons,
Finds that the Republic of Cameroon has violated the provisions of Articles 2, 3, 7(1)(d), 9, 10, 11, 13 and 26 of the Charter. Consequently:
The Republic of Kenya (Kenya) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights (African Charter or Charter), having ratified the Charter on 23 January 1992.

Pursuant to Article 62 of the African Charter, Kenya submitted its initial Report to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) at its 41 Ordinary Session, held in Accra, Ghana, from 16 to 30 May 2007.

The present Report, which was submitted in December 2014, is the 8-11 Periodic State Report of Kenya (covering the period 2008 to September 2014), and it brings Kenya up-to date with its reporting obligations provided for under Article 62 of the African Charter.

The Report was presented to the Commission by the delegation from Kenya led by Ms. Maryann Njau Kimani, Senior Deputy Solicitor General at the Office of the Attorney General and Department of Justice of Kenya.

The Report highlights developments which took place in Kenya in the promotion and protection of human rights, and the legislative, administrative and judicial measures put in place to comply with its obligations under the African Charter.

The present Concluding Observations and Recommendations give an account of the positive aspects, the factors restricting the enjoyment of human rights and the areas of concern regarding exercise of human rights in Kenya. The Commission makes recommendations to the Government of Kenya on measures for strengthening the enjoyment of human rights as guaranteed by the African Charter, as well as other relevant regional and international human rights instruments. The Commission notes a number of positive aspects in Kenya’s efforts towards the fulfilment of its obligations under the African Charter:

The Commission: i. welcomes the efforts made by Kenya in preparing and presenting its Report and commends the latter for being up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter; ii. commends the efforts made by Kenya to ensure that the preparatory process of the Periodic Report was participatory and transparent, with wide consultation between Government Officials, Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and Independent National Human Rights Institutions (NHRIs), for ensuring compliance with the African Charter, using a participatory and transparent process; and iii. commends Kenya for implementing some of the recommendations of the Commission in its Concluding Observations on Kenya’s Initial Periodic Report.
The Commission commends Kenya for ratifying the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol) in October 2010.

The Commission commends Kenya for the enactment of the following laws, amongst others, to guarantee human rights: i. The Constitution of Kenya of 2010; ii. The Commission commends Kenya on: i. Vision 2030, which is the country’s developmental blue print on which specific government policies are based, covers aspects that are relevant to human rights such as: access to adequate social amenities, including housing, water and sanitation infrastructure, and the need to improve human settlement systems; ii. Legislative, policy and other measures taken to guarantee the right of access to adequate housing, to ensure security of tenure for all citizens, particularly for the vulnerable and marginalized; including availability of utilities, economic and physical accessibility as well as cultural acceptability; iii. the establishment of the Uwezo Fund Initiative (UWEZO) which creates more jobs for women and the youth; iv. the Sessional Paper Number 4 of 2015 on National Employment Policy and Strategy for Kenya, passed by Parliament in August 2015 with a goal to promote decent jobs in the country through various identified multi-sectoral strategies, which, when implemented will go a long way in addressing unemployment challenges in Kenya; v. the increase in the number of hospitals from 167 in 2008 to 275 in 2012; vi. the introduction of free maternal health care in public hospitals in 2013 in order to encourage pregnant mothers to deliver in hospitals attended by skilled workers as opposed to delivering at home in a bid to reduce the high infant and maternal mortality rate; vii. the Traditional Health Practitioners Bill 2015 which is currently in Parliament and provides for the regulation of the practice of traditional medicine; viii. taking measures to enhance education in the informal settlements, with the Government providing capitation grants to 474 non-formal schools; ix. on the free primary and secondary school education; and the establishment of a National Council for Nomadic Education in 2015 which amongst other things reviews and develops policies in all matters relating to nomadic education; mobilizes funds for the development of nomadic education; and determines standards and skills to be attained in schools and institutions with nomadic communities.

The Commission commends Kenya for the: i. progressive jurisprudence of the Kenyan Judiciary with regards to determining cases relating to the citizen’s right to vote, especially on the right of prisoners to vote; ii. NGEC which promotes the principles of: impartiality, gender equality; inclusiveness, non-discrimination and protection of marginalized groups; and ongoing amendment of the Elections and Political Parties Act to address the challenges experienced for Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) in the 2013 general elections, including protection from violence and lack of funding to the PWDs. Women and Children’s Rights

The Commission commends Kenya on the: i. efforts made to reduce maternal and infant mortality rate in the country, especially the introduction of free maternal health care in public hospitals and improved access to and utilization of reproductive health services by economically disadvantaged populations; ii. sum of about 100 million which has been raised to establish mobile clinics to provide integrated HIV, maternal and child outreach services in the country; iii. department of Children’s Services, the National Council for Children Services, the KNCHR and the NGEC that work closely to ensure the realization of children’s rights in the country; iv. Division of Child and Adolescent Health established by the Ministry of Public Health and Sanitation mandated to promote and participate in the provision of an integrated and high quality promotive, preventive and rehabilitative health care for all children and adolescents; as well as ensures survival, growth development of children under the age of 5 years, health promotion in all children between 0-18 years, promotes good nutrition for children, expectant and nursing mothers and the health rights of the child; v. Child Survival Development Strategy 2008-2015, aimed at ensuring delivery of efficient and effective services to improve the lives of women and children; vi. establishment of day care centers in prisons and provision of social workers to look after the children of female inmates, as well as Family Days where children visit their parents in prison thus providing an opportunity for the families to bond; vii. National Plan of Action against Sexual Exploitation of Children in Kenya- 2013-2017; and the Sexual Offences Rules of Court, published by the Chief Justice which represents a key milestone in the development of the criminal law in the country; viii. establishment of the Anti-Female Genital Mutilation Board responsible for the implementation of the Female Genital Mutilation Act No. 32 of 2011; and ix. National Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Working Group established in 2014 which has commemorated 16 days of activism with the launch of the National GBV Campaign dubbed ‘Keeping the Promise to End GBV’. The campaign targets duty bearers and seeks to increase awareness on GBV in Kenya, hold duty bearers accountable to their roles, influence budget allocation and ultimately contribute to reduction of GBV cases in the country.
The Commission notes the draft Guidelines on Safe Abortion.

The Commission commends Kenya on the: i. enactment of the Kenya Information and Communications Act, CAP 411A which provides a framework for the establishment of e-Government, a portal where one can access Government documents and information; ii. increase in the use of technology and social media in the country; iii. increase in public access to Government information which enhances transparency and accountability; iv. appointment of Board of Directors for the Communications Authority selected by an independent panel comprising nominees from the private sector; and v. establishment of the Communications and Multimedia Appeals Tribunal to hear Complaints about any publication by or conduct of a journalist or media enterprise and anything done against a journalist or media enterprise that limits or interferes with the constitutional freedom of expression of such journalist or media enterprise.

The Commission commends Kenya for Article 37 of the Constitution which allows every person the right, to assemble, peaceably and unarmed, to demonstrate, and to present petitions to public authorities.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. efforts made in providing mechanisms to guarantee the payment of compensation to persons who have spent unlawful time in pre-trial detention; ii. structural development programs for prisons with a view to improving prison conditions through infrastructural upgrades and civil works in many prison facilities countrywide; iii. police oversight through the establishment of the IPOA; iv. plans to establish human rights desks in police stations in line with recommendations of the Police Reform Taskforce, and the establishment of gender desks in all police stations to make services accessible to gender violence survivors to seek redress easily; v. human rights training for Police Officers; and vi. structural reforms and institutional framework for averting the threat of terrorism in the police service through the Security Laws Amendment Act, of 2014 which provides a County Coordinating Commander to oversee the operations of all the services at the County level and enabled unity of command in combating terrorism.

The Commission commends Kenya for : i. a Code of Practice on Disability Mainstreaming in Public Service; ii. the establishment of a cash transfer program for vulnerable older persons aged 65 and above and persons with severe disabilities with the targeted beneficiaries receiving a monthly stipend of Ksh 2000 to cushion them against poverty; iii. a pilot programme for a health cover under the NHIF for older persons benefiting from the cash transfer, involving 500 beneficiaries who are spread across all Counties covering older persons on inpatient and outpatient, including reasonable accommodation; iv. ensuring that all public organizations include measurable targets in their performance contract every year on actions they intend to take to mainstream persons with disabilities (PWDs); v. the National Action Plan on Accessibility and Disabilities Rights which is a practical step in establishing a framework for a coordinated approach to implementing the PWDs Act, and related legislations touching on PWDs; and vi. subsidiary legislations to give effect to the PWDs Act, including: The PWDs (Access to Employment, Services and Facilities) Regulations 2009; The PWDs (Cost Care, Support and Maintenance) Regulations 2009; The PWDs (Registration) Regulations 2009; The PWDs (Income Tax Deductions and Exemptions) Order 2010; and the PWDs (National Development Fund for Persons with Disabilities) (Conduct of Business and Affairs of the Board of Trustees) Regulations 2009.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. the various legislative, policy, administrative and other measures reported to have been undertaken to give effect to the right to health, and in particular, for the prevention, management and control of HIV and AIDS, as well as for the legal protection and access to legal remedies for People Living With HIV (PLHIV) and those at risk, vulnerable to and affected by HIV; ii. the development of a Monitoring and Evaluation Framework 2014-15 to 2018-19 which provides a monitoring and evaluation framework for the HIV programme and Kenya AIDS Strategic Framework in general; iii. the establishment of the Equity (HIV and AIDS) Tribunal under the HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act, to determine complaints arising from breaches of this law; iv. free treatment services to all PLHIV in all public health facilities, including free testing, maternal health care, ARVs, free assistance from the HIV Tribunal and the provision of free Mobile Clinics; and v. the Anti Stigma Campaign of September 2015 which seeks to fast track the HIV response to end new infections, AIDs related deaths and stigma and discrimination in adolescents and young people, with an objective to reduce stigma and discrimination by 25%.

The Commission congratulates Kenya for its efforts in safeguarding the right to life including by observing a moratorium on death penalty since 1987, the commutation of death penalty to life imprisonment as well as efforts to raise public awareness on death penalty together with the KNCHR.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. implementing the Commission’s recommendation in Kenya’s initial State Report, urging the Government to take measures to cater for special needs of children with disabilities and integrate refugee children and internally displaced children in the regular school system.; ii. issuing visas and permits to migrant workers; and iii. the Refugee Bill of 2015 which provides for proper management of refugee matters including administrative, registration processes, residence of refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya, movement of refugees inside and outside Kenya, refugees right to work in Kenya, dealing with rejected asylum seekers, exclusion and disqualification grounds etc.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. establishing a Taskforce on the Implementation of the Commission’s Endorois decision, with a mandate to provide guidance on the political, security and economic implications of the decision, and examine the potential environmental impacts on Lake Bogoria and the surrounding area; and ii. ensuring the political participation of indigenous peoples in various organs of the Government.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. the ratification of the CAT and the inclusion of the prohibition of torture in Kenya’s 2010 Constitution; ii. enacting the 2014 Victim Protection Act, and for recently unveiling a memorial to victims of torture and ill-treatment during British colonial rule, which is an aspect of reparation to the victims; and iii. setting up a Working Group to prepare the Prevention of Torture Bill to implement the CAT and Constitutional provisions on the absolute prohibition of torture; criminalization of torture and other cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and has heavy penalties for contravention.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. having legislations safeguarding and protecting exploitation of natural resources and the environment which provide a legislative framework to manage and regulate the energy sector, and provide strategic oversight over all mining activities in the country; ii. its Mining Strategy 2030 which uses the Africa Mining Vision as model framework to improve mining activities in the country; iii. the establishment of the Environment and Land Court to hear and determine disputes relating to the environment and the use and occupation of, and title to land, and to make provision for its jurisdiction, functions and powers; iv. the social and environmental impact assessment which enables participation of affected communities; and v. availing public hearings to enable people give their views about issues of compensation, as well as free and informed consent.

The Commission commends Kenya for: i. increased border security control including inter-agency officials such as Immigration Officials, Kenya Revenue Authority and the Security Organs that have enhanced border security by ensuring that those entering the country are vetted at the border; and ii. intelligence-led policing which has enabled better access to actionable information on impending attacks especially along the borders at the Coastal and Northern Kenya.
Acts of terrorism in Kenya has seriously impeded the promotion and protection of human rights in the country.
The Security Laws (Amendment Act) of 2014 which inhibits the protection of human rights in the country, in particular freedom of expression.
Harmful cultural and traditional practices which continue to restrict Kenyan women and children from fully enjoying their rights.
Lack of knowledge by the majority of the population about regional and international human rights instruments ratified by Kenya which restricts the effective enjoyment of human rights in the country.
While acknowledging the significant efforts made by the Government of Kenya to promote and protect human rights, the Commission is however concerned about the following matters:

The Commission appreciates Kenya’s response to its recommendations in Kenya’s Initial Periodic Report of 2007. It however notes that, the current Report does not provide specific and comprehensive answers to some of the questions and issues raised by the Commission.

The Report does not for instance, provide comprehensive disaggregated data, including gender disaggregated data on its implementation of the rights guaranteed in the African Charter in order to allow the Commission to objectively assess Kenya’s level of compliance vis-à-vis the obligations contained in the African Charter.

Kenya has not ratified the following human rights instruments: i. The African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (the Kampala Convention); ii. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; iii. The Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights. iv. The African Union Convention on the Elimination of Mercenaries in Africa; v. International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of all Migrant Workers and Members of their Families; vi. The Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman and Degrading Treatment or Punishment (OPCAT); vii. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and viii. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
Kenya has also not made the Declaration under Article 34(6) of the Protocol to the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights, accepting the jurisdiction of the Court.

The Commission is concerned about: i. challenges associated with land use, which have increased in both urban and rural areas as a result of rapid urbanization, inadequate land use planning, and unsustainable production methods as well as poor environmental management; ii. the issue of adequate housing which remains a major challenge in Kenya, wherein majority of the residents in Kenya’s largest urban centres: Nairobi, Mombasa, and Kisumu live in informal settlements characterized by low quality of housing with poor infrastructural services, overcrowding, inadequate access to water or electricity, poor sanitary conditions, insecurity, lack of privacy and poor accessibility in times of disasters; iii. unemployment and underemployment which have been identified as Kenya’s most difficult and persistent challenges; iv. lack of integration of culture in the formal education system which impedes cultural creativity and expression; and v. lack of monitoring and effective regulation of private school chains, such as Bridge International Academies that register as non-formal schools, whereas they appear to offer formal education.

The Commission is concerned about the lack of information in the Report regarding adequate awareness of the population about their rights, legal procedures and available remedies in respect of their civil and political rights.

The Commission is concerned about: i. the low representation of women at decision making levels and gender inequality, despite the concerted efforts made at ensuring gender equality in all sectors, policies and programmes; ii. the persistent traditional harmful practices such as FGM and child marriages, in spite of the criminalization of the said practices; iii. the fact that child labour still remains a challenge due to poverty; and iv. Kenya’s non-implementation of the State Reporting Guidelines under the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission is concerned about: i. laws limiting freedom of expression such as the Security Laws (Amendment Act) of 2014 recently passed in Kenya which contains a number of provisions not in conformity with fundamental human rights, in particular those which unduly restrict freedom of expression; ii. the fact that defamation is still a criminal offence in the Criminal Code, and the use of defamation to incriminate journalists and media practitioners; and iii. lack of an Access to Information Law.
The Commission is concerned about lack of sufficient information in the Report concerning the protection of these rights.

The Commission is concerned about the: i. lack of statistics as to how many cases referred to the Director of Public Prosecution by the IPOA have been prosecuted; ii. lack of information regarding a database on torture-related complaints in Police Stations; iii. absence of legal aid provided to suspects at the time of police inquiry; iv. high rate of Pre-trial detainees; and v. lack of speedy processes in the judicial system which continues to hinder the right to fair trial.

The Commission is concerned about lack of specific legislation to protect the rights of older persons apart from the draft Older Persons Bill of 2015 which is yet to be adopted by Parliament, and the National Policy on Older Persons which was still pending for review before the end of 2015 as at the time of presentation of this Report.

The Commission is concerned that: i. even though the budget allocation of the Kenyan health sector has been increasing gradually, this allocation remains inadequate; and ii. the Report does not indicate measures put in in place by the State to support children orphaned by and other vulnerable children affected by HIV/AIDS.
The Commission is concerned that the death penalty remains in the Criminal Code despite the self-imposed moratorium on the death penalty.
The Commission is concerned that, i. the Refugee Bill of 2015 which provides for proper management of refugee matters is still pending adoption; and ii. IDPs are still not fully resettled.

The Commission is concerned that: i. even though Kenya established a Taskforce on the Implementation of the Endorois Case in September 2014, CSOs and Members of the Endorois Community are not part of the Taskforce. It is only composed of Members from the public sector including representatives from the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development, Ministry of Sports, Culture and the Arts, the Secretary to the KNCHR and the County Government of the affected area; ii. the Report does not contain information regarding measures taken by the Government to protect indigenous peoples and ensure their security, investigate and act on the reported cases of harassment, assault, violence and forced eviction against indigenous peoples, particularly sexual abuse against women during the disarmament exercises conducted in 2009, 2012, 2014 and 2015 in the Tana Delta Region and Northern Kenya, affecting the Turkana, Samburu, Pokot, Pokomo and Orma communities; and iii. although the Government has done a commendable work in ensuring the political participation of indigenous peoples in various organs of the Government, smaller indigenous groups such as the Ogiek of Mount Elgon, Ilchamus, and Emolo still lack formal representation and participation in the political affairs of the State.

The Commission is concerned that: i. the State has still not enacted the Prevention of Torture Bill (2014), initially Bill (2011); ii. there is no data in the Report in respect of the numbers of victims of torture in the country; and iii. the Government has not implemented decisions of the high court to compensate victims and survivors of torture

The Commission is concerned that: i. although the Mining Bill provides a framework for recognition, operations and regulation of artisanal miners, artisanal mining is considered illegal under the current Mining Law; and ii. illegal mining activities with seizures of illegal consignments of minerals; illegal mining and exports of gemstones, gold, copper and manganese from the country continue to take place due to loopholes in law, regulations and poor enforcement regimes, in addition to the fact that penalty under the existing law is too weak to deter these activities.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission makes the following recommendations to the Government of Kenya:
Kenya should ensure it complies with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter by implementing these recommendations.

Kenya should make a declaration under Article 34(6) of the Court Protocol and ratify the following human rights instruments: i. The Kampala Convention; ii. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; iii. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; iv. The Protocol of the Court of Justice and Human Rights of the African Union; v. The African Union Convention on the Elimination of Mercenaries in Africa; vi. The International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of all Migrant Workers and Members of their Families; vii. The OPCAT; viii. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and ix. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Social and Economic Rights

Kenya should: i. provide adequate housing for the urban and rural population as well as improve the existing urbanization pattern in identified developing and approved urban areas of the country; ii. ensure urban and rural-level infrastructure, including roadways, and water distribution; iii. implement Sessional Paper Number 4 of 2015 on National Employment Policy and Strategy for Kenya; create employment opportunities and skills training; iv. ensure culture-based educational strategies to encourage culturally competent and linguistically appropriate exchanges and collaborations among families, professionals, students, and communities. This will foster equitable outcomes for all students and result in the identification and provision of services that are responsive to issues of race, culture, gender, and social and economic status; and v. ensure monitoring of Bridge International Academies regarding their system and methods of education.

Kenya should include in its next Report, information in respect of legal procedures and available remedies on the civil and political rights of the population, and also include civic education in school curricula if this is not already done. Women and Children’s Rights

Kenya should: i. implement the Constitutional principle of the Political Parties Act, that not more than 2/3 majority shall belong to the same gender, so as to guarantee equal opportunities in the political spheres, particularly for women; ii. enact a comprehensive equality and non-discrimination law; iii. end traditional practices such as FGM and child marriages by supplementing existing laws that criminalize the said practices with other strategies such as proactive multi-faceted strategies at the national and community levels including inter alia; empowering girls with information, skills and support networks; educate and rally parents and community members; iv. cease the practice of child labour; v. fast track the Law on Safe Abortion and resolve some of the obstacles impeding the passing of the law by sensitising religious leaders on the consequences of unsafe abortion; vi. finalize the draft Guidelines on Safe Abortion; and vii. comply with the Commission’s State Reporting Guidelines under the Maputo Protocol.

Kenya should: i. decriminalize defamation by repealing relevant provisions in the Penal Code; ii. expedite the finalization and enactment of the draft Freedom of Information Bill; and iii. take appropriate measures to effectively guarantee the right to freedom of expression, in particular for journalists and human rights defenders.

Kenya should: i. provide more information on the above rights during its next Report; ii. take legislative and other measures in order to protect, and promote human rights in conformity with the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders, the African Charter, the Kigali Declaration and other regional and international human rights instruments that guarantee the right to freedom of association and assembly; and iii. provide adequate information on several rights with respect of which the Report provided no data on measures taken for the fulfilment of those rights.

Kenya should: i. ensure that the office of the Director of Public Prosecution provides statistics as to how many cases referred to them by the IPOA have been prosecuted; ii. establish a database on torture-related complaints in order to determine the prevalence of torture in Police Stations; iii. effectively implement domestic laws and policies on bail, bond and sentencing to reduce overcrowding in prisons and resultant problems of violence and adverse health consequences; iv. ensure speedy processes in the judicial system, and take appropriate measures to ensure strict respect of the 48 hours duration of police custody while reviewing the regime of pre-trial detention to comply with international standards such as the Commission’s Guidelines on Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-trial Detention (the Luanda Guidelines); v. continue to ensure human rights training for the police and other law enforcement officers; vi. make use of the Luanda Guidelines while providing training to the Police on the Guidelines, and adopting relevant laws and policies; and vii. extend access to legal services to suspects in Police Custody (specifically referring to the various ways of providing legal access as listed in Part 2. 8 of the Luanda Guidelines).
Kenya should expedite the enactment of the draft Older Persons Bill of 2015 and the National Policy on Older Persons.

Kenya should: i. ensure better management and increase of healthcare budget, and solve resource allocation problems by ensuring the use of systematic formulae for allocating funds so as to satisfy the equity criteria; and ii. include information and statistics on children orphaned by HIV/AIDs and other vulnerable children affected by HIV/AIDS in its next Report as well as measures taken to support them.
Kenya should abolish the death penalty and revise the Criminal Code accordingly.
Kenya should expedite the finalisation and adoption of the Refugee Bill of 2015 which provides for proper management of refugee matters in the country.

Kenya should: i. implement the Endorois decision, as non-implementation further contributes to discrimination and marginalization of these communities. In line with this, the Government should also ensure that the Task Force includes CSOs and the Endorois Community; ii. include information on human rights abuse against indigenous peoples, especially on the communities aforementioned and measures taken by the Government to investigate and punish the perpetrators; iii. ensure political participation of all indigenous communities; and iv. take urgent measures to address indigenous peoples’ specific needs in relation to land, education, health, employment and access to justice, and further ensure that affirmative action policies and measures adopted in this respect effectively and adequately benefit them.

Kenya should: i. fast-track the passing of the Prevention of Torture Bill, 2014 to ensure protection of all victims of torture and effective prevention and response to torture and ill-treatment in conformity with the holistic perspective envisaged in the Robben Island Guidelines; and ii. include data in its next Report in respect of the numbers of victims of torture in the country, and ensure prompt, impartial investigations and prosecution of perpetrators of torture.

Kenya should: i. implement measures to transform artisanal gold miners into formalized operators by adopting Artisanal Mining policies to regulate artisanal mining, thereby promoting miners in that sector to make reasonable contribution to sustainable development, economic growth and poverty alleviation in the country; and ii. put in place a legal framework regarding its natural resources with clear penalties for illegal practices so as to eradicate illegal mining activities in the country.

In light of Kenya’s history of violence, an Organized Crimes Division should be established in the High Court, to provide a forum where perpetrators can be prosecuted and victims seek redress, including in relation to the post-election violence of 2007 and 2008.

Kenya Government should: i. invite the Commission and its Special Mechanisms to undertake a promotional mission to the country; ii. provide, in its next periodic report, up-to-date statistics and data on all relevant sectors as well as on activities of institutions with a human rights mandate; and iii. inform the Commission, in its next periodic report, of the measures taken to address the above issues of concern and to ensure the effective implementation of the recommendations contained in the present Concluding Observations.
